html:
The campaign of 711 to 713 in which the Umayyad Caliphate conquered Sindh, the lower Indus valley in today's Pakistan. It made Sindh the first part of South Asia ruled by a Muslim state.

The young general Muhammad ibn Qasim led the army, sent by al-Hajjaj, governor of Iraq. The pretext was an attack by pirates on Muslim ships near the port of Debal. He took Debal, then defeated and killed Raja Dahir, last king of the Chach dynasty, and advanced as far as Multan in the Punjab.

The same years saw Umayyad armies cross into Spain: the caliphate reached its widest limits at both ends of the known world. Sindh stayed a frontier province. Local Hindus and Buddhists mostly kept their faiths as protected subjects paying tax. Arab rule did not spread further into India for centuries; the next big push came from Afghanistan with Mahmud of Ghazni around 1000 and later the Delhi Sultanate. Sindh also became a channel for Indian science, such as the numerals that reached Baghdad.
sum: The campaign of 711 to 713 in which the Umayyad Caliphate conquered Sindh, the lower Indus valley in today's Pakistan. It made Sindh the first part of South Asia ruled by a Muslim state.
